extracted.intended_audience: student reporters and working newspaper reporters (news-room journalists)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for organizing reporting notes and composing effective leads for news stories, including orders of organization (time, descriptive, expository, suspense) and detailed rules for writing summarizing and informal leads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organize notes before writing
rubrics_metrics.description: For speed and efficiency in composition and for accuracy, fairness, clearness, and interest in the story the reporter should organize his notes according to some definite plan before he begins to write.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start organizing as soon as you finish gathering facts; have notes grouped so you can write without pausing to study them. You need not use an outline, but go over material carefully, delete trivial details, and jot down important points in the order you plan to mention them. Preliminary preparation is of the utmost importance and should never be slighted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speed in composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Speed in composition is an asset as valuable as quickness in gathering news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Turn out copy quickly and avoid false starts at the typewriter. Notes taken during events are rarely logical; reorganizing them before writing prevents wasted time and mistakes. Example guideline: ten minutes of organization on the way to the office will save twenty minutes at the typewriter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Efficiency (discriminate significant vs trivial)
rubrics_metrics.description: Preliminary arrangement of material allows the reporter to estimate the relative importance of facts and to avoid overplaying some and underplaying others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disorderly notes lead to haphazard writing that is too full in places and meager in others. Well-arranged notes reduce the chance of heavy cutting by the copy reader and help the reporter gain a reputation for efficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy (reduce errors and libel risk)
rubrics_metrics.description: Organized notes reduce the likelihood of serious mistakes and help the reporter keep his mind on the development of the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Breaking off to search disorganized notes causes lost concentration and errors; hurried composition from unorganized notes is a common cause of libel suits. Only one thing can be done well at a time—arrange notes so attention can be concentrated on writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fairness (present both sides)
rubrics_metrics.description: Properly organized notes help the reporter present both sides of a controversy and avoid imparting bias by emphasis or omission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliberate warping violates the newspaper code; careless distortion through poor note handling can be equally damaging. Organize notes so both sides are apparent and can be presented fairly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clearness (keep time and space relations clear)
rubrics_metrics.description: Orderly arrangement of story parts prevents confusion; the reporter must keep time and space relations perfectly clear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present facts in the exact order you want readers to receive them. Clever arrangement of story phases can produce desired effects; logically arranged notes produce unity and coherence and a clear-cut impression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interest (enable vividness and tone)
rubrics_metrics.description: Organization of material contributes to interest in the story by freeing the reporter to concentrate on narrative tone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: With notes arranged so they can be read at a glance, the reporter can keep attention on weaving the narrative. Vividness, emphasis, and appeal cannot be created when the writer's mind is on mechanics of finding facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Four orders of organization
rubrics_metrics.description: There are four orders of organization: the simple time order; the descriptive order; the expository (complex) order; and the suspense order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Time order is used in about 95% of stories; descriptive and expository orders are used rarely; suspense about 3% in leading papers. Orders can be combined; no strict demarcation exists between them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time order (inverted pyramid practice)
rubrics_metrics.description: In describing a simple series of events, follow natural chronological sequence as far as possible, but put the most striking facts first so the story can be shortened without destroying sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present main facts complete in opening paragraphs because subsequent editions may shorten the story. If difficult to both put important facts first and keep strict time order, describe the important events first in chronological order and then add minor details in sequence, using transition sentences to indicate time relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Descriptive (space) order
rubrics_metrics.description: The descriptive order is that of simple space relations: present objects in the order of their placement from a stated point of view.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show the point of view at the beginning and keep to it; avoid dragging readers back and forth—escort them around a scene as you would escort someone physically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expository (complex) order
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin with things known and proceed to things unknown; the order of increasing complication, useful for explaining processes or scientific problems to lay readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start from familiar ideas and lead gradually to unfamiliar ones (e.g., explaining an invention or experiment). Use logical progression as in classroom exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suspense (climactic) order
rubrics_metrics.description: The suspense order is the short-story order: outcome of incidents is not revealed until the last part of the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use sparingly—suitable only when a series of events has strong dramatic punch. It is difficult to use and was once taboo in newspapers; reserve for special feature interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose order to suit speed, accuracy, interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Select the order of organization best suited to speed, accuracy, and interest; every story lends itself readily to some order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study notes intelligently; avoid following fads that distort sequence for unusual effects—such practice is bad and not tolerated by editors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of a strong beginning (the lead)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a story is read through often depends on the attention-arresting qualities of its opening sentences (the lead).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pick out the most striking features and play them up in a lively, curiosity-exciting beginning. The lead is usually small (one sentence, rarely more than two or three paragraphs) but outweighs the body in importance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of leads: summarizing vs informal
rubrics_metrics.description: Leads are of two types: the summarizing lead, which tells the gist and answers who, what, how, when, where, why; and the informal lead, which piques curiosity without summarizing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Summarizing leads are easier and more commonly used. Informal leads may be more playful and curiosity-provoking but require care.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summarizing lead must have the facts (who, what, how, when, where, why)
rubrics_metrics.description: Before writing a summarizing lead, make sure you have who, what, how, when, where, and why; select the cardinal point deserving emphasis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the feature of greatest interest and present it at the beginning of the lead rather than burying it. Arrange facts to give 'punch' and human interest even in a summarizing lead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arrange lead details to feature the most interesting point
rubrics_metrics.description: The order of details in a lead may be changed to play up different points (who, what, why, how, when, where).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the element to emphasize (feature interest). Examples show different orders and discuss which choices are effective. When in doubt, consult the city editor; ordinarily study facts intelligently to decide.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lead should not be overburdened
rubrics_metrics.description: The lead should never be burdened with minor details or attempt to tell the whole story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compression is essential; if the whole story is told in the lead, nothing more should be written. Avoid long involved constructions and repetition; prefer ten short emphatic sentences to one long overloaded one.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liveliness improves the lead
rubrics_metrics.description: Adding a touch of human interest or liveliness can brighten a dull story and attract readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid stereotyped openings; a clever informal turn (not too far-fetched) can make even routine items readable. Balance liveliness so it does not appear strained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lead must be complete
rubrics_metrics.description: Although leads should not overload with minor details, the summarizing lead must answer all fundamental questions about the event—omitting one can make an account inaccurate or misleading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure there is a who, a what, a when, and a where in every story; include why and how when they are relevant to the occurrence.
